Pattern 20 of 24

Shortest Path & MST

When edges have costs, plain BFS no longer finds the cheapest route. A min-heap fixes that: always expand the cheapest thing you know about next. Dijkstra uses it to find shortest paths; Prim uses it to connect everything as cheaply as possible.

1. What is this pattern for?

Planning a road trip with a map that shows driving times. BFS counts roads: it would happily take three short hops over one long highway even if the highway is faster overall. Dijkstra counts minutes: it keeps a "closest city not yet visited" list and always drives to that one next, so when it reaches a city, no shorter route can still be waiting.

Two classic heap-driven algorithms on weighted graphs:

  • Dijkstra (single-source shortest paths). Distances from one start to every node, when all edge weights are non-negative. Network delay, cheapest flights (without a stop limit), path with minimum effort, swim in rising water.
  • Prim (minimum spanning tree, MST). The cheapest set of edges that connects all nodes, with no single start and end. Connect all points, cheapest cabling.

They look almost identical in code. The only difference is the number pushed onto the heap: Dijkstra pushes the total distance from the start, Prim pushes just the edge weight.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Build an adjacency list node → [(neighbour, weight), …] (or compute edges on the fly for a complete graph of points).
  2. Push the start onto a min-heap: (0, start).
  3. Pop the cheapest entry. If its node is already settled, skip it (a stale entry). Otherwise settle it: its value is final.
  4. Relax its edges. Push (dist + w, nbr) for Dijkstra, or (w, nbr) for Prim, for every unsettled neighbour.
  5. Stop when the heap is empty (Dijkstra) or when every node is in the tree (Prim).

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot Shortest Path / MST

Trigger words

  • "minimum time / cost / effort to reach", "network delay", "cheapest path" with weights
  • "signal reaches all nodes", "how long until everyone receives it"
  • "connect all points / cities / houses with minimum total cost"
  • "minimum spanning tree", "every pair connected"
  • a grid where moving into a cell costs its value or the height difference

Shape of the input

  • An edge list (u, v, w) with w ≥ 0, or points whose pairwise distance is the cost.
  • A grid treated as a graph with per-move costs.
  • Brute-force smell: BFS that ignores weights, or trying every path / every subset of edges.
The one question to ask"Do edges have different non-negative costs, and do I need the cheapest route (Dijkstra) or the cheapest way to connect everything (Prim)?"

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use Dijkstra / Prim when…Prefer something else when…
Weights differ and are non-negativeEvery edge costs the same: plain BFS is simpler and O(V + E)
You need shortest distances from one sourceEdges can be negative: Bellman–Ford (also handles "at most k stops")
You must connect all nodes at minimum total costEdges are given as a sparse list: Kruskal (sort edges + union-find) is often easier
A grid with per-cell costs (minimum effort, swim in water)Weights are only 0 or 1: 0-1 BFS with a deque

Cost: O(E log E) time with a binary heap and lazy deletion, O(V + E) space. On a complete graph of n points, Prim is O(n² log n) with a heap, or O(n²) with a simple array.

5. The templates, step by step (Python, TypeScript, Java)

Both templates grow a set of "finished" nodes using a min-heap, and both use the lazy trick: push duplicates freely, and skip any entry whose node is already finished when it's popped. A (Dijkstra) orders the heap by total distance from the start, giving shortest paths with non-negative weights. B (Prim) orders it by the single edge's cost, growing a minimum spanning tree. Same loop, one different number in the heap.

TypeScript has no built-in heap. The TypeScript templates on this page use this small MinHeap class (Python has heapq, Java has PriorityQueue). 
class MinHeap<T> {
  items: T[] = [];
  less: (x: T, y: T) => boolean;
  constructor(less: (x: T, y: T) => boolean) { this.less = less; }
  get size(): number { return this.items.length; }
  peek(): T | undefined { return this.items[0]; }
  push(x: T): void {
    const a = this.items;
    a.push(x);
    for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; ) {            // bubble up
      const p = (i - 1) >> 1;
      if (!this.less(a[i], a[p])) break;
      [a[i], a[p]] = [a[p], a[i]];
      i = p;
    }
  }
  pop(): T | undefined {
    const a = this.items, top = a[0], last = a.pop()!;
    if (a.length > 0) {
      a[0] = last;
      for (let i = 0; ; ) {                            // sink down
        const l = 2 * i + 1, r = l + 1;
        let m = i;
        if (l < a.length && this.less(a[l], a[m])) m = l;
        if (r < a.length && this.less(a[r], a[m])) m = r;
        if (m === i) break;
        [a[i], a[m]] = [a[m], a[i]];
        i = m;
      }
    }
    return top;
  }
}

Pass a "less than" function: new MinHeap<number>((a, b) => a < b) is a min-heap, (a, b) => a > b a max-heap. Push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1).

Template A · Dijkstra (shortest paths, non-negative weights)

The question it answersShortest distance from start to every node when edges have non-negative weights.
What it keepsA min-heap of (distance so far, node); dist for finished nodes.
When it checks for an answerA node is finished the first time it's popped; later (stale) entries for it are skipped.
Use it whenNetwork delay (LC 743), cheapest path with weights, path with minimum effort (LC 1631, on a grid).
Not forNegative weights (Bellman-Ford); unweighted graphs (BFS, page 12, is simpler).
Memory hook: "Always settle the closest unsettled town next"Planning trips from home: of all towns you know a route to, the closest one can't get any closer (every other route is already longer and weights aren't negative), so settle it and look at its roads. Repeat.

The story, mapped to the code. Nodes are towns; weights are road lengths.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Known routes, closest firstheap of (d, node)Min-heap by total distance.
Settle the closestd, node = heappop(heap)Its distance is final.
Already settledif node in dist: continueA stale, longer route: skip.
Write it downdist[node] = dFinal.
Offer longer routesheappush(heap, (d + w, nbr))Through this town.

The template. Lazy Dijkstra: no decrease-key, just skip stale entries.

import heapq

def dijkstra(graph, start):
    dist = {}
    heap = [(0, start)]
    while heap:
        d, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if node in dist:
            continue
        dist[node] = d
        for nbr, w in graph[node]:
            if nbr not in dist:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (d + w, nbr))
    return dist
function dijkstra(graph: number[][][], start: number): Map<number, number> {
  const dist = new Map<number, number>();
  const heap = new MinHeap<number[]>((a, b) => a[0] < b[0]);
  heap.push([0, start]);
  while (heap.size > 0) {
    const [d, node] = heap.pop()!;
    if (dist.has(node)) continue;
    dist.set(node, d);
    for (const [nbr, w] of graph[node]) {
      if (!dist.has(nbr)) heap.push([d + w, nbr]);
    }
  }
  return dist;
}
static Map<Integer, Integer> dijkstra(List<List<int[]>> graph, int start) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> dist = new HashMap<>();
    PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    heap.offer(new int[]{0, start});
    while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
        int[] top = heap.poll();
        int d = top[0], node = top[1];
        if (dist.containsKey(node)) continue;
        dist.put(node, d);
        for (int[] e : graph.get(node)) {
            if (!dist.containsKey(e[0])) heap.offer(new int[]{d + e[1], e[0]});
        }
    }
    return dist;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
d, node = heapq.heappop(heap)The closest known route.Settle the closest town.A FIFO queue here gives wrong answers with weights.
if node in dist: continueSkips stale entries.Already settled: this route is longer.Without it, a stale entry overwrites the true distance (see the bug player).
dist[node] = dFinal distance.Write it down.—
heapq.heappush(heap, (d + w, nbr))Offers a route through node.Longer routes via this town.Pushing (w, nbr) is Prim, not Dijkstra.

Watch it run. Step through the graph from node 0. The second player removes the stale-entry check.

Node 1 is first settled at 3 (via 2). Its older entry (4, 1) is popped later; without the skip it overwrites dist[1] with 4 and pushes worse routes: the result is [0, 4, 1, 6, 9] instead of [0, 3, 1, 4, 7].

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. Nodes are settled in non-decreasing order of distance; when a node is popped for the first time, its distance is the shortest possible (requires weights ≥ 0).

Complexity. O(m log m) time (each edge may push one entry), O(n + m) space.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Negative weights. The "closest can't get closer" argument fails.
  • No stale check. Settle each node once.
  • Pushing edge weight instead of total. Heap key = distance from start.

The line people get wrong
if node in dist: continue.

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

dist to 4 in the example?

7 (0→2→1→3→4).

Why is the first pop final?

Every other route is already at least as long; weights can't shrink it.

Grid version?

Same loop; neighbours are the 4 cells.

Template B · Prim (minimum spanning tree)

The question it answersCheapest set of edges that connects all n nodes (total cost).
What it keepsA min-heap of (edge cost, node); in_tree.
When it checks for an answerA popped node already in the tree is skipped; otherwise its edge joins the tree.
Use it whenMin cost to connect points (LC 1584), network cabling, dense graphs.
Not forShortest paths (A). For sparse edge lists, Kruskal + Union-Find (page 23) is often simpler.
Memory hook: "Grow the island by its cheapest bridge"Building bridges from an island: of all bridges that would connect a new town, build the cheapest. The island grows by one town each time. Bridges to towns already on the island are skipped.

The story, mapped to the code. The tree is an island growing from node 0.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Bridges off the islandheap of (cost, node)Cheapest first.
Already on the islandif node in in_tree: continueSkip.
Build the bridgein_tree.add(node); total += costGrow by one.
New bridgesheappush(heap, (cost, nbr))Single edge cost, not a total.

The template. Same loop as Dijkstra; the heap key is the edge cost alone.

import heapq

def prim(n, graph):
    in_tree, total = set(), 0
    heap = [(0, 0)]
    while len(in_tree) < n:
        cost, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if node in in_tree:
            continue
        in_tree.add(node)
        total += cost
        for nbr, w in graph[node]:
            if nbr not in in_tree:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (w, nbr))
    return total
function prim(n: number, graph: number[][][]): number {
  const inTree = new Set<number>();
  let total = 0;
  const heap = new MinHeap<number[]>((a, b) => a[0] < b[0]);
  heap.push([0, 0]);
  while (inTree.size < n) {
    const [cost, node] = heap.pop()!;
    if (inTree.has(node)) continue;
    inTree.add(node);
    total += cost;
    for (const [nbr, w] of graph[node]) {
      if (!inTree.has(nbr)) heap.push([w, nbr]);
    }
  }
  return total;
}
static int prim(int n, List<List<int[]>> graph) {
    Set<Integer> inTree = new HashSet<>();
    int total = 0;
    PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
    heap.offer(new int[]{0, 0});
    while (inTree.size() < n) {
        int[] top = heap.poll();
        int cost = top[0], node = top[1];
        if (inTree.contains(node)) continue;
        inTree.add(node);
        total += cost;
        for (int[] e : graph.get(node)) {
            if (!inTree.contains(e[0])) heap.offer(new int[]{e[1], e[0]});
        }
    }
    return total;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
heap = [(0, 0)]Start the island at node 0 with a free "bridge".The first town costs nothing.—
if node in in_tree: continueSkips bridges to towns already joined.Already on the island.Without it, cycles add extra cost.
heapq.heappush(heap, (w, nbr))Key = this edge's cost only.A bridge's own price.Pushing total + w turns it into Dijkstra and no longer finds the MST.
while len(in_tree) < nStops when every node is in.All towns connected.A disconnected graph empties the heap first: check for that.

Watch it run. Same graph as A. Compare which edges each template picks.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. The chosen edges always form a tree on in_tree, and the cheapest edge leaving that tree is always in some MST (cut property).

Complexity. O(m log m) time, O(n + m) space.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Pushing total distance. Prim compares single edges.
  • Disconnected input. Detect an empty heap before all nodes are in.

On the example both settle the same nodes but for different reasons: Dijkstra's distance to 4 is 7 (a path), Prim's total is also 7 (a tree) — a coincidence of this graph. The single changed number in the push is the whole difference.

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Closest unvisited city next"Pop the cheapest, settle it, push its neighbours. Dijkstra pushes the trip total; Prim pushes just the last road.
How this hook works: what “Closest unvisited city next” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Closest unvisited city next”
Always settle the node with the smallest known total distance. That node is final, because every road is non-negative, so a detour can't come back cheaper.
“Pop the cheapest, settle it, push its neighbours”
The loop: heappop, skip it if already settled, record it, push the neighbours.
“Dijkstra pushes the trip total; Prim pushes just the last road”
The same loop answers two questions: shortest paths (key = d + w) and minimum spanning tree (key = w).

Why this picture fits the pattern: Weighted graphs break BFS: fewer roads isn't the same as fewer minutes. A min-heap that always hands you the closest unsettled city fixes that, and the hook says what goes into the heap for each of the two algorithms.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
Cities you could drive to nextheap of (distance, node)
The closest oned, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
Already visitedif node in dist: continue
Settle itdist[node] = d
Dijkstra: trip totalheappush(heap, (d + w, nbr))
Prim: just the last roadheappush(heap, (w, nbr))

Watch it on numbers

Roads A–B 4, A–C 1, C–B 2, B–D 1. Start at A.

  1. Settle A at 0. Push B (4) and C (1).
  2. Closest is C (1): settle it. Push B via C: 1 + 2 = 3.
  3. Closest is B (3, not 4): settle it. Push D: 4.
  4. Pop B (4): already settled, so skip this stale entry. Settle D at 4. Result A 0, C 1, B 3, D 4.

The trap it saves you from

Negative edges break "settled is final" (use Bellman-Ford). Not skipping stale heap entries does wasted or wrong work. Running BFS on weighted edges finds the fewest roads, not the cheapest route.

It still works when…

Network Delay Time is the largest settled distance. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops adds the stop count to the state. Min Cost to Connect All Points is Prim: push only the last road.

Picture

Ink spreading on paper that soaks in faster along cheap edges: each node turns dark at exactly its shortest distance.

Chant

"Pop, skip if seen, settle, push. Total for Dijkstra, edge for Prim."

Safety rule

"No negative edges." Dijkstra's "settled is final" breaks if an edge can lower a distance later.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

New to this pattern? Start with theseSolve 743. Network Delay Time, then 1584. Min Cost to Connect All Points, then 1631. Path With Minimum Effort. They are marked Start here below. Read the explanation, press Play on the step-through, then close the page and solve it yourself on LeetCode.
Medium 743. Network Delay Time Start here Google Nvidia Amazon Netflix GraphHeap

Problem: times[i] = (u, v, w) is a directed edge from node u to v taking w time. A signal starts at k. Return the time until all n nodes have received it, or -1 if some never do.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: times = [[2,1,1],[2,3,1],[3,4,1]], n = 4, k = 2
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: times = [[1,2,1]], n = 2, k = 1
Output: 1

Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ times.length ≤ 6000 · times[i].length == 3 · 1 ≤ ui, vi ≤ n · ui != vi · 0 ≤ wi ≤ 100 · All the pairs (ui, vi) are unique. (i.e., no multiple edges.)

Hint 1

You need the shortest travel time from k to every node, with different edge weights.

Hint 2

Dijkstra with a min-heap; the answer is the largest shortest time, or −1 if some node is unreachable.

From brute force to the pattern: BFS ignores weights; trying all paths is exponential; Bellman–Ford is O(V · E). With non-negative weights Dijkstra is O(E log E).

Spot it: Shortest travel times from one source with non-negative weights → Dijkstra. The answer is the largest of those shortest times (the last node to hear the signal).

Approach:

  1. Build an adjacency list u → [(v, w), …].
  2. Push (0, k) onto a min-heap. dist stores each node's final shortest time.
  3. Pop the smallest time. If that node is already settled, skip it; otherwise settle it and push (time + w, v) for every unsettled neighbour.
  4. If all n nodes are settled, return the largest time; else -1.
import heapq

class Solution:
    def networkDelayTime(self, times: List[List[int]], n: int, k: int) -> int:
        graph = {}
        for u, v, w in times:
            if u not in graph:
                graph[u] = []
            graph[u].append((v, w))
        dist = {}                      # node -> final shortest time
        heap = [(0, k)]                # (time so far, node)
        while heap:
            time, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if node in dist:
                continue               # already settled by a faster route
            dist[node] = time
            for nxt, w in graph.get(node, []):
                if nxt not in dist:
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (time + w, nxt))
        if len(dist) < n:
            return -1                  # some node never received the signal
        return max(dist.values())
function networkDelayTime(times: number[][], n: number, k: number): number {
    const graph = new Map<number, [number, number][]>();
    for (const [u, v, w] of times) {
        if (!graph.has(u)) {
            graph.set(u, []);
        }
        graph.get(u)!.push([v, w]);
    }
    const dist = new Map<number, number>();  // node -> final shortest time
    // [time so far, node], smallest first
    const heap = new Heap<[number, number]>((a, b) => (a[0] !== b[0] ? a[0] < b[0] : a[1] < b[1]));
    heap.push([0, k]);
    while (heap.size > 0) {
        const [time, node] = heap.pop();
        if (dist.has(node)) {
            continue;  // already settled by a faster route
        }
        dist.set(node, time);
        for (const [nxt, w] of graph.get(node) ?? []) {
            if (!dist.has(nxt)) {
                heap.push([time + w, nxt]);
            }
        }
    }
    if (dist.size < n) {
        return -1;  // some node never received the signal
    }
    return Math.max(...dist.values());
}


// ---- helper: a small binary heap (TypeScript has no built-in priority queue) ----
// `less(a, b)` decides which item comes out first. The player doesn't step inside it.
class Heap<T> {
    private items: T[] = [];
    private less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean;

    constructor(less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean) {
        this.less = less;
    }

    get size(): number {
        return this.items.length;
    }

    peek(): T {
        return this.items[0];
    }

    push(x: T): void {
        const a = this.items;
        a.push(x);
        let i = a.length - 1;
        while (i > 0) {
            const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
            if (!this.less(a[i], a[parent])) {
                break;
            }
            [a[i], a[parent]] = [a[parent], a[i]];
            i = parent;
        }
    }

    pop(): T {
        const a = this.items;
        const top = a[0];
        const last = a.pop()!;
        if (a.length > 0) {
            a[0] = last;
            let i = 0;
            while (true) {
                const l = 2 * i + 1;
                const r = l + 1;
                let m = i;
                if (l < a.length && this.less(a[l], a[m])) {
                    m = l;
                }
                if (r < a.length && this.less(a[r], a[m])) {
                    m = r;
                }
                if (m === i) {
                    break;
                }
                [a[i], a[m]] = [a[m], a[i]];
                i = m;
            }
        }
        return top;
    }
}
class Solution {
    public int networkDelayTime(int[][] times, int n, int k) {
        Map<Integer, List<int[]>> graph = new HashMap<>();
        for (int[] t : times) {
            graph.computeIfAbsent(t[0], key -> new ArrayList<>()).add(new int[] {t[1], t[2]});
        }
        Map<Integer, Integer> dist = new HashMap<>();  // node -> final shortest time
        // (time so far, node), smallest first
        PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]) : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        heap.offer(new int[] {0, k});
        while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
            int[] top = heap.poll();
            int time = top[0], node = top[1];
            if (dist.containsKey(node)) {
                continue;  // already settled by a faster route
            }
            dist.put(node, time);
            for (int[] edge : graph.getOrDefault(node, List.of())) {
                if (!dist.containsKey(edge[0])) {
                    heap.offer(new int[] {time + edge[1], edge[0]});
                }
            }
        }
        if (dist.size() < n) {
            return -1;  // some node never received the signal
        }
        return Collections.max(dist.values());
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. graph: adjacency list of outgoing edges with their weights.
  2. heap = [(0, k)]: tuples compare by their first item, so the heap always pops the smallest known time.
  3. if node in dist: continue: a node can be pushed several times with different times; only the first pop (the smallest) counts. This "lazy deletion" replaces a decrease-key operation.
  4. dist[node] = time: final. With non-negative weights, no later route can be shorter than the smallest time on the heap.
  5. heapq.heappush(heap, (time + w, nxt)): a candidate time for each neighbour.
  6. if len(dist) < n: return -1, else max(dist.values()): everyone must be reached, and the slowest arrival is the answer.

Dry run on the example:

times = [[2, 1, 1], [2, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1]], n = 4, k = 2 (LeetCode Example 1). Returns 2.

pop (time, node)actionpusheddist after
(0, 2)settle 2(1, 1), (1, 3){2: 0}
(1, 1)settle 1 (no outgoing edges)—{2: 0, 1: 1}
(1, 3)settle 3(2, 4){2: 0, 1: 1, 3: 1}
(2, 4)settle 4 (no outgoing edges)—{2: 0, 1: 1, 3: 1, 4: 2}

All 4 nodes are settled; the largest time is 2.

Edge cases to test:

  • An unreachable node → −1.
  • A single node → 0.
  • Several edges between the same pair.

Complexity: O(E log E) time with a binary heap, O(V + E) space.

Medium 1584. Min Cost to Connect All Points Start here Google Amazon GraphHeap

Problem: Connect all points on a plane so every pair is connected by some path. The cost of an edge between two points is their Manhattan distance |x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|. Return the minimum total cost.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: points = [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]]
Output: 20
Explanation: We can connect the points as shown above to get the minimum cost of 20. Notice that there is a unique path between every pair of points.
Example 2
Input: points = [[3,12],[-2,5],[-4,1]]
Output: 18

Constraints: 1 ≤ points.length ≤ 1000 · -10⁶ ≤ xi, yi ≤ 10⁶ · All pairs (xi, yi) are distinct.

Hint 1

Connecting everything at minimum total cost is a minimum spanning tree.

Hint 2

Prim's algorithm: grow from point 0, always adding the cheapest edge out of the tree (min-heap keyed by Manhattan distance).

From brute force to the pattern: Trying all spanning trees is exponential. Prim's with a heap is O(n² log n) on this complete graph (or O(n²) with an array); Kruskal sorts the n² edges.

Spot it: "Connect everything as cheaply as possible" is a minimum spanning tree. The graph is complete (every pair can be connected), so Prim's algorithm, which grows one tree from a start point, is a natural fit.

Approach:

  1. Start the tree with point 0: push (0, 0) = (cost to attach, point) onto a min-heap.
  2. Pop the cheapest entry. If that point is already in the tree, skip it. Otherwise add it and its cost to the total.
  3. Push (distance, j) for every point j not yet in the tree.
  4. Stop when all points are in the tree.
import heapq

class Solution:
    def minCostConnectPoints(self, points: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(points)
        in_tree = [False] * n
        heap = [(0, 0)]          # (cost to attach this point, point index)
        total = 0
        added = 0
        while added < n:
            cost, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if in_tree[i]:
                continue         # already attached more cheaply
            in_tree[i] = True
            total = total + cost
            added = added + 1
            xi, yi = points[i]
            for j in range(n):
                if not in_tree[j]:
                    xj, yj = points[j]
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (abs(xi - xj) + abs(yi - yj), j))
        return total
function minCostConnectPoints(points: number[][]): number {
    const n = points.length;
    const inTree: boolean[] = new Array(n).fill(false);
    // [cost to attach this point, point index], smallest first
    const heap = new Heap<[number, number]>((a, b) => (a[0] !== b[0] ? a[0] < b[0] : a[1] < b[1]));
    heap.push([0, 0]);
    let total = 0;
    let added = 0;
    while (added < n) {
        const [cost, i] = heap.pop();
        if (inTree[i]) {
            continue;  // already attached more cheaply
        }
        inTree[i] = true;
        total = total + cost;
        added = added + 1;
        const [xi, yi] = points[i];
        for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) {
            if (!inTree[j]) {
                const [xj, yj] = points[j];
                heap.push([Math.abs(xi - xj) + Math.abs(yi - yj), j]);
            }
        }
    }
    return total;
}


// ---- helper: a small binary heap (TypeScript has no built-in priority queue) ----
// `less(a, b)` decides which item comes out first. The player doesn't step inside it.
class Heap<T> {
    private items: T[] = [];
    private less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean;

    constructor(less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean) {
        this.less = less;
    }

    get size(): number {
        return this.items.length;
    }

    peek(): T {
        return this.items[0];
    }

    push(x: T): void {
        const a = this.items;
        a.push(x);
        let i = a.length - 1;
        while (i > 0) {
            const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
            if (!this.less(a[i], a[parent])) {
                break;
            }
            [a[i], a[parent]] = [a[parent], a[i]];
            i = parent;
        }
    }

    pop(): T {
        const a = this.items;
        const top = a[0];
        const last = a.pop()!;
        if (a.length > 0) {
            a[0] = last;
            let i = 0;
            while (true) {
                const l = 2 * i + 1;
                const r = l + 1;
                let m = i;
                if (l < a.length && this.less(a[l], a[m])) {
                    m = l;
                }
                if (r < a.length && this.less(a[r], a[m])) {
                    m = r;
                }
                if (m === i) {
                    break;
                }
                [a[i], a[m]] = [a[m], a[i]];
                i = m;
            }
        }
        return top;
    }
}
class Solution {
    public int minCostConnectPoints(int[][] points) {
        int n = points.length;
        boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
        // (cost to attach this point, point index), smallest first
        PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]) : Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        heap.offer(new int[] {0, 0});
        int total = 0;
        int added = 0;
        while (added < n) {
            int[] top = heap.poll();
            int cost = top[0], i = top[1];
            if (inTree[i]) {
                continue;  // already attached more cheaply
            }
            inTree[i] = true;
            total = total + cost;
            added = added + 1;
            int xi = points[i][0], yi = points[i][1];
            for (int j = 0; j < n; j++) {
                if (!inTree[j]) {
                    heap.offer(new int[] {Math.abs(xi - points[j][0]) + Math.abs(yi - points[j][1]), j});
                }
            }
        }
        return total;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. in_tree: which points are already connected.
  2. heap = [(0, 0)]: attaching the first point is free.
  3. if in_tree[i]: continue: a point can be on the heap several times; only its cheapest entry (popped first) is used.
  4. total = total + cost: the cheapest edge leaving the tree is always safe to add. That's the cut property that makes Prim correct.
  5. for j in range(n): ... heappush(...): new candidate edges from the point we just added.
  6. while added < n: a spanning tree is finished when all n points are in it (n − 1 edges).

Dry run on the example:

points = [[0, 0], [2, 2], [3, 10], [5, 2], [7, 0]] (LeetCode Example 1). Returns 20.

pop (cost, point)actiontotal
(0, 0)add point 0 [0, 0]0
(4, 1)add point 1 [2, 2]4
(3, 3)add point 3 [5, 2]7
(4, 4)add point 4 [7, 0]11
(7, 3)already in the tree → skip11
(7, 4)already in the tree → skip11
(7, 4)already in the tree → skip11
(9, 2)add point 2 [3, 10]20

Edge cases to test:

  • A single point → 0.
  • Duplicate points (distance 0).
  • Collinear points.

Complexity: O(n² log n) time (up to n² heap pushes), O(n²) heap space. (An array-based Prim without a heap is O(n²) time, O(n) space.)

8. Common mistakes

Negative weightsDijkstra assumes a settled distance can never improve. A negative edge breaks that; use Bellman–Ford.
Settling when pushing instead of when poppingMarking a node done when it's first pushed locks in the first route found, not the shortest. Settle on pop.
Not skipping stale heap entriesWithout if node in dist: continue, a node is processed several times and its neighbours get wrong (too large) distances pushed again.
Using Dijkstra's total in PrimPrim must push the edge weight only. Pushing d + w builds a shortest-path tree, which is not the minimum spanning tree.
Forgetting unreachable nodes"Time for all nodes to receive the signal" is -1 if some node is never settled. Check len(dist) == n.

9. Self-check quiz

Shortest path in a grid where every move costs 1. Which algorithm?

With equal weights, BFS order is already distance order; a heap adds log factors for nothing.

In Dijkstra, when is a node's distance final?

The first pop carries the smallest value ever pushed for that node; with non-negative weights nothing smaller can appear later.

In Prim's algorithm, what number is pushed with a neighbour?

Prim grows a tree; the cost of adding a node is only the edge that attaches it.

The graph has a negative edge weight (but no negative cycle). Which algorithm still works?

Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge V − 1 times and doesn't rely on "settled is final".

Medium 787. Cheapest Flights Within K Stops Google Meta Amazon Cisco Apple Graph

Problem: Return the cheapest price from src to dst using at most k stops (k + 1 flights), or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 4, flights = [[0,1,100],[1,2,100],[2,0,100],[1,3,600],[2,3,200]], src = 0, dst = 3, k = 1
Output: 700
Explanation: The graph is shown above. The optimal path with at most 1 stop from city 0 to 3 is marked in red and has cost 100 + 600 = 700. Note that the path through cities [0,1,2,3] is cheaper but is invalid because it uses 2 stops.
Example 2
Input: n = 3, flights = [[0,1,100],[1,2,100],[0,2,500]], src = 0, dst = 2, k = 1
Output: 200
Explanation: The graph is shown above. The optimal path with at most 1 stop from city 0 to 2 is marked in red and has cost 100 + 100 = 200.

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 100 · 0 ≤ flights.length ≤ (n * (n - 1) / 2) · flights[i].length == 3 · 0 ≤ fromi, toi < n · fromi != toi · 1 ≤ pricei ≤ 10⁴ · There will not be any multiple flights between two cities. · 0 ≤ src, dst, k < n · src != dst

Hint 1

The limit is on the number of edges. Which shortest-path algorithm counts edges in rounds?

Hint 2

Run Bellman–Ford for k + 1 rounds; be careful to use the previous round's values.

From brute force to the pattern: DFS over all routes is exponential; limited Bellman–Ford is O(kE).

Spot it: A shortest path with a limit on the number of edges. Bellman–Ford's round i finds the best prices using at most i edges, so run exactly k + 1 rounds. Relax from a copy of the previous round so one round never chains two flights.

Why not another pattern? Plain Dijkstra ignores the stop limit: a cheaper path with too many stops can block a valid one.

Approach:

  1. price[src] = 0, others ∞.
  2. Repeat k + 1 times: new = price[:]; for each flight (u, v, w): new[v] = min(new[v], price[u] + w).
  3. Return price[dst] or −1.
class Solution:
    def findCheapestPrice(self, n: int, flights: List[List[int]], src: int, dst: int, k: int) -> int:
        INF = float("inf")
        price = [INF] * n
        price[src] = 0
        for _ in range(k + 1):  # at most k + 1 flights
            new = price[:]  # read old values so each round adds only one flight
            for u, v, w in flights:
                if price[u] + w < new[v]:
                    new[v] = price[u] + w
            price = new
        return price[dst] if price[dst] < INF else -1
function findCheapestPrice(n: number, flights: number[][], src: number, dst: number, k: number): number {
    const INF = Infinity;
    let price: number[] = new Array(n).fill(INF);
    price[src] = 0;
    for (let round = 0; round <= k; round++) {  // at most k + 1 flights
        const next = [...price];  // read old values so each round adds only one flight
        for (const [u, v, w] of flights) {
            if (price[u] + w < next[v]) {
                next[v] = price[u] + w;
            }
        }
        price = next;
    }
    return price[dst] < INF ? price[dst] : -1;
}
class Solution {
    public int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
        final int INF = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        int[] price = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(price, INF);
        price[src] = 0;
        for (int round = 0; round <= k; round++) {  // at most k + 1 flights
            int[] next = price.clone();  // read old values so each round adds only one flight
            for (int[] f : flights) {
                int u = f[0], v = f[1], w = f[2];
                if (price[u] != INF && price[u] + w < next[v]) {
                    next[v] = price[u] + w;
                }
            }
            price = next;
        }
        return price[dst] < INF ? price[dst] : -1;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. After round i, price[v] is the cheapest cost using at most i flights.
  2. Reading from price (old) while writing to new prevents using two flights in one round.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • src == dst.
  • A cheap route with too many stops.
  • No route → −1.

Complexity: O(k · E) time, O(n) space.

Medium 1514. Path with Maximum Probability Google GraphHeap

Problem: Edges have success probabilities. Return the maximum probability of a path from start_node to end_node.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]], succProb = [0.5,0.5,0.2], start = 0, end = 2
Output: 0.25000
Explanation: There are two paths from start to end, one having a probability of success = 0.2 and the other has 0.5 * 0.5 = 0.25.
Example 2
Input: n = 3, edges = [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]], succProb = [0.5,0.5,0.3], start = 0, end = 2
Output: 0.30000

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10^4 · 0 ≤ start, end < n · start != end · 0 ≤ a, b < n · a != b · 0 ≤ succProb.length == edges.length ≤ 2*10^4 · 0 ≤ succProb[i] ≤ 1 · There is at most one edge between every two nodes.

Hint 1

How does a path's probability change as it gets longer?

Hint 2

That's like non-negative edge weights: use Dijkstra with max instead of min.

From brute force to the pattern: Bellman–Ford is O(VE); Dijkstra is O(E log V).

Spot it: Multiplying by numbers ≤ 1 never increases the probability, just as adding non-negative weights never decreases a distance → Dijkstra with a max-heap.

Why not another pattern? BFS ignores weights; Bellman–Ford is O(VE).

Approach:

  1. best[start] = 1; heap of (−prob, node).
  2. Pop the most probable node; skip stale entries; stop at the end node.
  3. Relax: p · edge_prob > best[v] → update and push.
import heapq

class Solution:
    def maxProbability(self, n: int, edges: List[List[int]], succProb: List[float], start_node: int, end_node: int) -> float:
        adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]
        for (a, b), p in zip(edges, succProb):
            adj[a].append((b, p))
            adj[b].append((a, p))
        best = [0.0] * n
        best[start_node] = 1.0
        heap = [(-1.0, start_node)]  # max-heap via negation
        while heap:
            neg, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
            p = -neg
            if u == end_node:
                return p  # the first time we pop it, it's optimal
            if p < best[u]:
                continue  # stale entry
            for v, q in adj[u]:
                if p * q > best[v]:
                    best[v] = p * q
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (-best[v], v))
        return 0.0
function maxProbability(n: number, edges: number[][], succProb: number[], start_node: number, end_node: number): number {
    const adj: [number, number][][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => []);
    edges.forEach(([a, b], i) => {
        adj[a].push([b, succProb[i]]);
        adj[b].push([a, succProb[i]]);
    });
    const best: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    best[start_node] = 1.0;
    // [probability, node]: highest probability first, then smallest node
    const heap = new Heap<[number, number]>((a, b) => (a[0] !== b[0] ? a[0] > b[0] : a[1] < b[1]));
    heap.push([1.0, start_node]);
    while (heap.size > 0) {
        const [p, u] = heap.pop();
        if (u === end_node) {
            return p;  // the first time we pop it, it's optimal
        }
        if (p < best[u]) {
            continue;  // stale entry
        }
        for (const [v, q] of adj[u]) {
            if (p * q > best[v]) {
                best[v] = p * q;
                heap.push([best[v], v]);
            }
        }
    }
    return 0.0;
}


// ---- helper: a small binary heap (TypeScript has no built-in priority queue) ----
// `less(a, b)` decides which item comes out first. The player doesn't step inside it.
class Heap<T> {
    private items: T[] = [];
    private less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean;

    constructor(less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean) {
        this.less = less;
    }

    get size(): number {
        return this.items.length;
    }

    peek(): T {
        return this.items[0];
    }

    push(x: T): void {
        const a = this.items;
        a.push(x);
        let i = a.length - 1;
        while (i > 0) {
            const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
            if (!this.less(a[i], a[parent])) {
                break;
            }
            [a[i], a[parent]] = [a[parent], a[i]];
            i = parent;
        }
    }

    pop(): T {
        const a = this.items;
        const top = a[0];
        const last = a.pop()!;
        if (a.length > 0) {
            a[0] = last;
            let i = 0;
            while (true) {
                const l = 2 * i + 1;
                const r = l + 1;
                let m = i;
                if (l < a.length && this.less(a[l], a[m])) {
                    m = l;
                }
                if (r < a.length && this.less(a[r], a[m])) {
                    m = r;
                }
                if (m === i) {
                    break;
                }
                [a[i], a[m]] = [a[m], a[i]];
                i = m;
            }
        }
        return top;
    }
}
class Solution {
    public double maxProbability(int n, int[][] edges, double[] succProb, int start_node, int end_node) {
        List<List<double[]>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            adj.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }
        for (int i = 0; i < edges.length; i++) {
            adj.get(edges[i][0]).add(new double[] {edges[i][1], succProb[i]});
            adj.get(edges[i][1]).add(new double[] {edges[i][0], succProb[i]});
        }
        double[] best = new double[n];
        best[start_node] = 1.0;
        // (probability, node): highest probability first, then smallest node
        PriorityQueue<double[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Double.compare(b[0], a[0]) : Double.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        heap.offer(new double[] {1.0, start_node});
        while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
            double[] top = heap.poll();
            double p = top[0];
            int u = (int) top[1];
            if (u == end_node) {
                return p;  // the first time we pop it, it's optimal
            }
            if (p < best[u]) {
                continue;  // stale entry
            }
            for (double[] edge : adj.get(u)) {
                int v = (int) edge[0];
                double q = edge[1];
                if (p * q > best[v]) {
                    best[v] = p * q;
                    heap.offer(new double[] {best[v], v});
                }
            }
        }
        return 0.0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Probabilities only shrink along a path, which is what makes Dijkstra's greedy choice valid.
  2. Stale heap entries are skipped by comparing with best.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No path → 0.
  • start == end → 1 (not in constraints but handled).
  • Several paths with equal probability.

Complexity: O(E log V) time, O(V + E) space.

Medium 1631. Path With Minimum Effort Start here Google Amazon MatrixHeap

Problem: A path's effort is its largest absolute height difference between consecutive cells. Return the minimum effort from top-left to bottom-right.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: heights = [[1,2,2],[3,8,2],[5,3,5]]
Output: 2
Explanation: The route of [1,3,5,3,5] has a maximum absolute difference of 2 in consecutive cells. This is better than the route of [1,2,2,2,5], where the maximum absolute difference is 3.
Example 2
Input: heights = [[1,2,3],[3,8,4],[5,3,5]]
Output: 1
Explanation: The route of [1,2,3,4,5] has a maximum absolute difference of 1 in consecutive cells, which is better than route [1,3,5,3,5].

Constraints: rows == heights.length · columns == heights[i].length · 1 ≤ rows, columns ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ heights[i][j] ≤ 10⁶

Hint 1

The cost of a path is its maximum step. Does Dijkstra still work with max instead of +?

Hint 2

Alternatively, binary-search the effort and check reachability with BFS.

From brute force to the pattern: All paths are exponential; binary search + BFS is O(mn log H); Dijkstra is O(mn log mn).

Spot it: Minimising a maximum along a path still works with Dijkstra: the cost max(effort so far, step) never decreases along a path.

Why not another pattern? Plain BFS ignores the costs; DP right/down only misses paths that go up or left.

Approach:

  1. effort[0][0] = 0; heap (0, 0, 0).
  2. Pop the smallest effort; for each neighbour: e = max(effort, |Δh|); if smaller, update and push.
  3. Return when the target is popped.
import heapq

class Solution:
    def minimumEffortPath(self, heights: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])
        effort = [[float("inf")] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
        effort[0][0] = 0
        heap = [(0, 0, 0)]
        while heap:
            e, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if (r, c) == (rows - 1, cols - 1):
                return e
            if e > effort[r][c]:
                continue  # stale
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols:
                    ne = max(e, abs(heights[nr][nc] - heights[r][c]))  # the path's worst step
                    if ne < effort[nr][nc]:
                        effort[nr][nc] = ne
                        heapq.heappush(heap, (ne, nr, nc))
        return 0
function minimumEffortPath(heights: number[][]): number {
    const rows = heights.length, cols = heights[0].length;
    const effort: number[][] = Array.from({ length: rows }, () => new Array(cols).fill(Infinity));
    effort[0][0] = 0;
    // [effort, row, col], smallest first
    const heap = new Heap<[number, number, number]>((a, b) => (a[0] !== b[0] ? a[0] < b[0] : a[1] !== b[1] ? a[1] < b[1] : a[2] < b[2]));
    heap.push([0, 0, 0]);
    while (heap.size > 0) {
        const [e, r, c] = heap.pop();
        if (r === rows - 1 && c === cols - 1) {
            return e;
        }
        if (e > effort[r][c]) {
            continue;  // stale
        }
        for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
            if (0 <= nr && nr < rows && 0 <= nc && nc < cols) {
                const ne = Math.max(e, Math.abs(heights[nr][nc] - heights[r][c]));  // the path's worst step
                if (ne < effort[nr][nc]) {
                    effort[nr][nc] = ne;
                    heap.push([ne, nr, nc]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}


// ---- helper: a small binary heap (TypeScript has no built-in priority queue) ----
// `less(a, b)` decides which item comes out first. The player doesn't step inside it.
class Heap<T> {
    private items: T[] = [];
    private less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean;

    constructor(less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean) {
        this.less = less;
    }

    get size(): number {
        return this.items.length;
    }

    peek(): T {
        return this.items[0];
    }

    push(x: T): void {
        const a = this.items;
        a.push(x);
        let i = a.length - 1;
        while (i > 0) {
            const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
            if (!this.less(a[i], a[parent])) {
                break;
            }
            [a[i], a[parent]] = [a[parent], a[i]];
            i = parent;
        }
    }

    pop(): T {
        const a = this.items;
        const top = a[0];
        const last = a.pop()!;
        if (a.length > 0) {
            a[0] = last;
            let i = 0;
            while (true) {
                const l = 2 * i + 1;
                const r = l + 1;
                let m = i;
                if (l < a.length && this.less(a[l], a[m])) {
                    m = l;
                }
                if (r < a.length && this.less(a[r], a[m])) {
                    m = r;
                }
                if (m === i) {
                    break;
                }
                [a[i], a[m]] = [a[m], a[i]];
                i = m;
            }
        }
        return top;
    }
}
class Solution {
    public int minimumEffortPath(int[][] heights) {
        int rows = heights.length, cols = heights[0].length;
        int[][] effort = new int[rows][cols];
        for (int[] row : effort) {
            Arrays.fill(row, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        }
        effort[0][0] = 0;
        // (effort, row, col), smallest first
        PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(a[0], b[0])
                : a[1] != b[1] ? Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]) : Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));
        heap.offer(new int[] {0, 0, 0});
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
            int[] top = heap.poll();
            int e = top[0], r = top[1], c = top[2];
            if (r == rows - 1 && c == cols - 1) {
                return e;
            }
            if (e > effort[r][c]) {
                continue;  // stale
            }
            for (int[] d : dirs) {
                int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                if (0 <= nr && nr < rows && 0 <= nc && nc < cols) {
                    int ne = Math.max(e, Math.abs(heights[nr][nc] - heights[r][c]));  // the path's worst step
                    if (ne < effort[nr][nc]) {
                        effort[nr][nc] = ne;
                        heap.offer(new int[] {ne, nr, nc});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The cost of extending a path is max, which is monotone, so Dijkstra's first pop of a cell is optimal.
  2. The answer is returned as soon as the target is popped.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • A 1×1 grid → 0.
  • A detour that avoids a big step.
  • All equal heights → 0.

Complexity: O(mn log(mn)) time, O(mn) space.

Medium 2812. Find the Safest Path in a Grid Google Meta MatrixQueueHeap

Problem: A path's safeness is the minimum distance from any of its cells to the nearest thief. Maximise it from (0, 0) to (n−1, n−1).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: grid = [[1,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,1]]
Output: 0
Explanation: All paths from (0, 0) to (n - 1, n - 1) go through the thieves in cells (0, 0) and (n - 1, n - 1).
Example 2
Input: grid = [[0,0,1],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]
Output: 2
Explanation: The path depicted in the picture above has a safeness factor of 2 since: - The closest cell of the path to the thief at cell (0, 2) is cell (0, 0). The distance between them is | 0 - 0 | + | 0 - 2 | = 2. It can be shown that there are no other paths with a higher safeness factor.

Constraints: 1 ≤ grid.length == n ≤ 400 · grid[i].length == n · grid[i][j] is either 0 or 1. · There is at least one thief in the grid.

Hint 1

First compute each cell's distance to the nearest thief.

Hint 2

Then find the path whose smallest distance is as large as possible.

From brute force to the pattern: BFS from every cell to find thieves is O(n⁴); multi-source BFS + Dijkstra is O(n² log n).

Spot it: Two steps: multi-source BFS from all thieves computes each cell's distance to the nearest thief. Then maximise the minimum along a path: Dijkstra with a max-heap (the bottleneck path).

Why not another pattern? Computing distances by BFS from every cell is O(n⁴).

Approach:

  1. BFS from all thieves at once: dist[r][c].
  2. Max-heap from (0, 0) with value dist[0][0]; the value of a path is min(path value, dist[cell]).
  3. Return when the target is popped.
import heapq
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def maximumSafenessFactor(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        dist = [[-1] * n for _ in range(n)]
        queue = deque()
        for r in range(n):
            for c in range(n):
                if grid[r][c] == 1:
                    dist[r][c] = 0  # every thief is a BFS source
                    queue.append((r, c))
        while queue:
            r, c = queue.popleft()
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and dist[nr][nc] < 0:
                    dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1
                    queue.append((nr, nc))
        best = [[-1] * n for _ in range(n)]
        best[0][0] = dist[0][0]
        heap = [(-dist[0][0], 0, 0)]  # max-heap on the path's safeness
        while heap:
            neg, r, c = heapq.heappop(heap)
            safe = -neg
            if (r, c) == (n - 1, n - 1):
                return safe
            if safe < best[r][c]:
                continue
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n:
                    s = min(safe, dist[nr][nc])  # the path is only as safe as its worst cell
                    if s > best[nr][nc]:
                        best[nr][nc] = s
                        heapq.heappush(heap, (-s, nr, nc))
        return 0
function maximumSafenessFactor(grid: number[][]): number {
    const n = grid.length;
    const dist: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(-1));
    const queue: [number, number][] = [];
    for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] === 1) {
                dist[r][c] = 0;  // every thief is a BFS source
                queue.push([r, c]);
            }
        }
    }
    let head = 0;  // queue[head] is the front (shift() would be O(n))
    while (head < queue.length) {
        const [r, c] = queue[head++];
        for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
            if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n && dist[nr][nc] < 0) {
                dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1;
                queue.push([nr, nc]);
            }
        }
    }
    const best: number[][] = Array.from({ length: n }, () => new Array(n).fill(-1));
    best[0][0] = dist[0][0];
    // [safeness, row, col]: safest first, then smallest row, col
    const heap = new Heap<[number, number, number]>((a, b) => (a[0] !== b[0] ? a[0] > b[0] : a[1] !== b[1] ? a[1] < b[1] : a[2] < b[2]));
    heap.push([dist[0][0], 0, 0]);
    while (heap.size > 0) {
        const [safe, r, c] = heap.pop();
        if (r === n - 1 && c === n - 1) {
            return safe;
        }
        if (safe < best[r][c]) {
            continue;
        }
        for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
            if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n) {
                const s = Math.min(safe, dist[nr][nc]);  // the path is only as safe as its worst cell
                if (s > best[nr][nc]) {
                    best[nr][nc] = s;
                    heap.push([s, nr, nc]);
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return 0;
}

// `less(a, b)` decides which item comes out first. The player doesn't step inside it.
class Heap<T> {
    private items: T[] = [];

    constructor(less: (a: T, b: T) => boolean) {

    get size(): number {

    }

    peek(): T {
        return this.items[0];
    }

    push(x: T): void {
        const a = this.items;
        a.push(x);

        while (i > 0) {
            const parent = (i - 1) >> 1;
            if (!this.less(a[i], a[parent])) {
                break;
            }
            [a[i], a[parent]] = [a[parent], a[i]];
            i = parent;
        }
    }

    pop(): T {
        const a = this.items;
        const top = a[0];
        const last = a.pop()!;
        if (a.length > 0) {
            a[0] = last;
            let i = 0;
            while (true) {
                const l = 2 * i + 1;
                const r = l + 1;
                let m = i;
                if (l < a.length && this.less(a[l], a[m])) {
                    m = l;
                }

                    m = r;
                }
                if (m === i) {

class Solution {
    public int maximumSafenessFactor(List<List<Integer>> grid) {
        int n = grid.size();
        int[][] dist = new int[n][n];
        for (int[] row : dist) {
            Arrays.fill(row, -1);
        }
        Deque<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                if (grid.get(r).get(c) == 1) {
                    dist[r][c] = 0;  // every thief is a BFS source
                    queue.offer(new int[] {r, c});
                }
            }
        }
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int[] cell = queue.poll();
            for (int[] d : dirs) {
                int nr = cell[0] + d[0], nc = cell[1] + d[1];
                if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n && dist[nr][nc] < 0) {
                    dist[nr][nc] = dist[cell[0]][cell[1]] + 1;
                    queue.offer(new int[] {nr, nc});
                }
            }
        }
        int[][] best = new int[n][n];
        for (int[] row : best) {
            Arrays.fill(row, -1);
        }
        best[0][0] = dist[0][0];
        // (safeness, row, col): safest first, then smallest row, col
        PriorityQueue<int[]> heap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] != b[0] ? Integer.compare(b[0], a[0])
                : a[1] != b[1] ? Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]) : Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));
        heap.offer(new int[] {dist[0][0], 0, 0});
        while (!heap.isEmpty()) {
            int[] top = heap.poll();
            int safe = top[0], r = top[1], c = top[2];
            if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) {
                return safe;
            }
            if (safe < best[r][c]) {
                continue;
            }
            for (int[] d : dirs) {
                int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n) {
                    int s = Math.min(safe, dist[nr][nc]);  // the path is only as safe as its worst cell
                    if (s > best[nr][nc]) {
                        best[nr][nc] = s;
                        heap.offer(new int[] {s, nr, nc});
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Multi-source BFS layer d is exactly the cells at distance d from the nearest thief.
  2. Safeness along a path only decreases (min), so Dijkstra with a max-heap finds the best bottleneck.
